about.title: Live Oak Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Live Oak's economy runs on agriculture, food processing, and the trucks and equipment that move goods along Rt 99 and the surrounding rural roads. Those same conditions — heavy machinery, forklifts, delivery vehicles, packing lines — create real risk for the people who work them. If you're hurt on the job here, California generally routes you through workers' compensation first, regardless of who caused the accident. But that's not always the end of the story. If a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver played a role in what happened, a separate claim against that third party may be possible alongside your workers' comp benefits. Sorting out which path applies — and whether more than one applies — is exactly the kind of question an independent attorney can help answer. LawProactive doesn't charge for the connection, and the attorneys in our network work on contingency, so there's no upfront cost to get clarity on your situation.

whyChoose.title: Why Live Oak Workers Turn to LawProactive

items.title: Third-Party Claims Aren't Off the Table
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but if a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker contributed to your injury, a separate claim may be possible. An attorney can help you see whether that applies to your case.

items.title: Deadlines Move Fast
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and any third-party claim carries its own 2-year deadline under California law. Missing either window can limit your options, so getting guidance early matters.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal
items.desc: California law prohibits employers from punishing workers for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you're worried about how reporting might be received, an independent attorney can explain your protections.

items.question: I was hurt while driving a company truck near Rt 99 — can I still file a workers' comp claim?
items.answer: Likely yes, since injuries during work-related driving are typically covered by workers' compensation regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, there may also be a separate third-party claim worth exploring. An attorney can look at the specifics and explain how the two claims might work together.

items.question: Does workers' comp cover everything, or can I sue my employer directly?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, meaning you generally can't sue them separately even if they were careless. The exception is when a third party outside your employer — like an equipment maker or another company's driver — contributed to the injury. That's when a separate claim can come into play.

items.question: What if my employer in Live Oak discourages me from reporting my injury?
items.answer: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury or filing a claim is illegal under California law. You still have 30 days to report the injury regardless of any pressure not to. An independent attorney can advise you on documenting what happened and protecting your rights.
